subject: Social Science
central_question: How did industrialisation develop through factories, hand labour, colonial control, small-scale production and market-making rather than through machines alone?
in_scope_units: Introduction: popular images of progress and the need to question a simple machine-centred history
Before the Industrial Revolution: proto-industrial production linking towns and countryside
The Coming Up of the Factory: cotton inventions, Richard Arkwright and production under one roof
The Pace of Industrial Change: the slow and uneven spread of machinery and the survival of traditional industries
Hand Labour and Steam Power: labour abundance, seasonality, specialised products and limited mechanisation
Life of the Workers: migration, unemployment, insecure work, poor relief and resistance to the Spinning Jenny
Industrialisation in the Colonies: India’s textile trade and the shift from old ports to colonial ports
What Happened to Weavers?: Company monopoly, gomasthas, advances, coercion and weaver resistance
Manchester Comes to India: imported cloth, collapsing markets and raw cotton shortages
Factories Come Up: early mills, entrepreneurs, capital and labour recruitment in India
The Peculiarities of Industrial Growth: export industries, swadeshi, wartime expansion and import substitution
Small-scale Industries Predominate: handloom survival, fly shuttles and specialised production
Market for Goods: labels, calendars, religious images, royal figures and swadeshi advertising
Conclusion: factories and machines grew, but hand production remained integral to industrialisation
banned_topics: The detailed history of print technology and censorship, which belongs to Print Culture and the Modern World
The complete history of global trade institutions after the Second World War
The political history of Indian nationalism except the swadeshi and wartime market effects stated in this chapter
Modern industrial policy after Indian independence

known_pitfalls.claim: Industrialisation began only when factories appeared.
known_pitfalls.correction: Large-scale production for international markets existed earlier through proto-industrial networks of merchants, peasants and artisans.

known_pitfalls.claim: Machines quickly replaced hand labour in nineteenth-century Britain.
known_pitfalls.correction: Technology spread slowly, labour was abundant and cheap, many products required skill, and traditional sectors remained important.

known_pitfalls.claim: East India Company advances gave weavers freedom and bargaining power.
known_pitfalls.correction: Advances tied weavers to the Company, prevented sales to other buyers and enabled coercive control through gomasthas.

known_pitfalls.claim: Indian factory growth destroyed handloom production completely.
known_pitfalls.correction: Handloom production survived and expanded in the twentieth century through specialised goods, stable elite demand and technologies such as the fly shuttle.

known_pitfalls.claim: Advertisements merely informed buyers about products.
known_pitfalls.correction: Manufacturers used labels, gods, royal figures, calendars and nationalist messages to create familiarity, trust, desire and new consumer needs.
